title: EOR vs PEO: What is the difference?
summary: Employer of record vs PEO: see which model legally employs your staff and when each one fits. Written for cross-border hiring teams. Compare both now.
body_markdown:
Hiring someone in another country sounds exciting until you start looking into employment laws, payroll taxes, contracts and local regulations. Suddenly, bringing one new person onto your team involves a lot more than sending an offer letter.


If you're expanding internationally, you've probably come across two options: an employer of record (EOR) and a professional employer organisation (PEO). Both help businesses manage employees, but they work in very different ways.


So, when comparing an employer of record vs PEO, which one makes more sense for your business?


An employer of record (EOR) legally employs staff on your behalf, allowing you to hire in another country without setting up a local company. A professional employer organisation (PEO) shares certain employment responsibilities with your existing business through co-employment. The biggest difference is who legally employs your workers and whether you need a registered local entity.


Let's look at how both models work, what they cost and how to choose the right one for your growing team.


## EOR vs PEO: How do they compare?


The easiest way to understand the difference between an EOR and a PEO is to look at who takes responsibility for employment.


An EOR becomes the legal employer of your workers in the relevant country, while a PEO works alongside your existing business to manage employment-related tasks.


Here's how the two compare:


Feature Employer of record (EOR) Professional employer organisation (PEO)


Legal employer EOR is the formal legal employer Your company remains an employer under a co-employment arrangement


Local entity required
No, typically not Yes, generally


Employment model
Third-party legal employment Co-employment


Geographic reach
Particularly useful for international hiring Commonly used for domestic HR management


Payroll
EOR administers local payroll PEO administers payroll on behalf of the client


Compliance EOR handles many formal employer obligations Responsibilities are shared according to the agreement and applicable law


Employee benefits EOR arranges locally compliant benefits PEO helps administer benefits and may provide access to group plans


Liability EOR assumes specified legal employer responsibilities, but the client retains some risks Responsibilities and liabilities are divided between the PEO and client


Best for Hiring in countries where you don't have a registered business Managing HR and payroll where your business already operates


Typical pricing
Often a monthly fee per employee Often a fee per employee or a percentage of payroll


‍


You may also see the term PEO employer of record used when researching international hiring. This can be confusing because a PEO may handle payroll administration and certain employer-related filings without becoming the sole legal employer of your staff.


The important thing is to check the actual employment arrangement, not just the terminology a provider uses.


## What is an EOR?


An employer of record (EOR) is a third-party organisation that legally employs workers on behalf of another company, allowing businesses to hire internationally without setting up a local entity.


Imagine you run a US-based technology company and find an excellent developer in the Philippines. You want to hire them full-time, but you don't have a registered company there or the infrastructure to manage local payroll and employment regulations.


An EOR becomes the developer's legal employer, taking care of these responsibilities while you manage their everyday work.


### How does an EOR work?


An EOR typically handles the legal and administrative aspects of employment, including:


- Preparing locally compliant employment contracts
- Processing salaries, taxes and statutory deductions
- Managing employee benefits, leave and contributions
- Handling onboarding, offboarding and employment compliance


Your company remains in charge of daily operations, including assigning tasks, managing performance and setting team goals.


This arrangement is particularly useful for businesses looking to explore new markets, build international teams or expand without investing in local subsidiaries.


However, working with an EOR doesn't remove all your legal responsibilities. Your company may still be accountable for workplace practices, intellectual property and data protection, depending on local laws and contractual arrangements.


For a closer look at the model, read our guide explaining[what an employer of record is](https://grey.co/blog/what-is-employer-of-record) .


## What is a PEO?


A professional employer organisation (PEO) shares certain employment responsibilities with your business through a co-employment arrangement. Unlike an EOR, a traditional PEO generally requires your company to have an existing legal entity in the country where your employees work.


Imagine you run a growing marketing agency in California with 30 employees, but managing payroll, benefits and HR paperwork is becoming increasingly time-consuming.


A PEO helps you manage these responsibilities while your company remains an employer.


### How does a PEO work?


A PEO typically helps businesses manage employment-related tasks, including:


- Processing payroll and managing tax filings
- Administering employee benefits
- Providing HR support and employment documentation
- Assisting with employment compliance


Your company continues to manage employees' daily work, performance and business decisions.


Working with a PEO may also give smaller businesses access to employee benefits that would otherwise be expensive or difficult to manage independently.


However, employment responsibilities are shared. Your company remains accountable for workplace practices, employee supervision and its obligations under applicable laws.


If you're exploring this option, our guide to[what a PEO is](https://grey.co/blog/what-is-a-peo) explains the model in more detail.


## Key differences between an EOR and a PEO


The main differences between an EOR and a PEO come down to four things: local entity requirements, geographic coverage, compliance responsibilities and costs.


**1. Local entity requirements**


An EOR allows you to hire employees in another country without establishing your own local entity, while a traditional PEO generally requires an existing registered business.


For example, if you're a US company hiring your first employee in Germany, an EOR may be the more practical option. If you already have a German subsidiary, a PEO or local HR outsourcing provider may be a better fit.


**2. Geographic coverage**


EOR services are designed for international hiring, allowing businesses to build teams across multiple countries without establishing a separate company in each location.


Traditional PEOs are more commonly used for domestic employment, particularly in the US.


Some providers offer international PEO services, but these may operate through an EOR or another employment structure. Always check which model applies in your target country.


**3. Compliance and legal responsibility**


An EOR becomes the formal legal employer, handling responsibilities such as employment contracts, payroll taxes and statutory contributions.


With a PEO, these responsibilities are shared between your company and the provider through a co-employment agreement.


Neither model removes all your legal obligations. Your business may still be responsible for workplace safety, employee classification and other employment matters.


The[US Department of Labor's guidance on joint employment](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/flsa/joint-employment) explains how employment responsibilities can extend to more than one organisation under certain US labour laws.


**4. Costs and pricing**


EOR providers typically charge a fixed monthly fee per employee, while PEOs often charge a fee per employee or a percentage of payroll.


For example, an EOR charging $500 per employee would cost $2,500 per month for five employees. A PEO charging $150 per employee would cost $750 for the same number of workers, assuming your business already has a local entity.


These figures are illustrative and exclude salaries, taxes, benefits and additional charges.


When comparing costs, look beyond the monthly fee. An EOR may be more expensive per employee but save you the cost of establishing and maintaining a foreign entity. A PEO may offer better value if your business is already established and you're looking to scale your HR operations.


## When should you choose an EOR or a PEO?


Choose an EOR if you want to hire employees in a country where you don't have a legal entity. A PEO is a better fit if your business is already established and needs support managing HR, payroll and employee benefits.


### **Choose an EOR when you're expanding internationally**


An EOR is particularly useful when hiring your first overseas employees, exploring new markets or building a global team.


Imagine your US-based software company wants to hire a designer in Brazil, a developer in India and a customer support specialist in the Philippines. Instead of establishing three separate legal entities, an EOR can manage local employment arrangements while you focus on running your team.


However, as your workforce grows in a particular country, establishing your own entity may become more cost-effective.


### **Choose a PEO when you're scaling an existing business**


A PEO makes sense when your business is growing and managing HR internally is becoming increasingly demanding.


For example, if your consulting firm has grown from 10 to 80 employees, a PEO can help manage payroll, benefits, onboarding and HR administration without the need to build a large internal HR department.


You get professional HR support while maintaining your existing employment structure.


### **What if you're hiring contractors instead?**


If you're working with independent contractors, you may not need an EOR or PEO. You can generally engage them directly through a service agreement and pay them for their work.


However, the working relationship must meet local classification rules. If someone follows a fixed schedule, works under direct supervision and operates like a regular employee, they may need to be classified as one.


Understanding the difference between a[contractor and an employee](https://grey.co/blog/contractor-vs-employee) can help you avoid legal and tax complications.


## Paying a global team: How does it work with an EOR or PEO?


With an EOR, you fund the provider, which handles local payroll. With a PEO, payroll is managed through your existing business and its agreed payroll arrangements.


When managing an international team, you'll also need to consider exchange rates, transfer fees and payment delivery times.


### Paying employees through an EOR


The payroll process with an EOR typically involves four steps:


1. Your company submits salary details and payroll adjustments.
2. The EOR calculates taxes, contributions and benefits.
3. Your company funds the EOR according to its invoice.
4. The EOR pays employees through the local payroll system.


For example, if your US company employs someone in Brazil, you might receive an invoice in USD while the employee gets paid in Brazilian reais.


Make sure you understand how your EOR handles currency conversion, funding deadlines and additional payroll fees.


### Paying employees through a PEO


A PEO manages payroll, tax deductions and employee benefits through your existing business's employment structure.


If you operate in multiple countries, you may need separate payroll arrangements for each location. A traditional US PEO, for example, won't necessarily handle payroll for employees in the Philippines or Kenya.


Check which countries your provider supports and what payment options are available.

### What should you check before paying an international team?


Before choosing a payment method, consider:


- Who is responsible for processing payroll and statutory deductions

Remember that paying a contractor's invoice is different from processing an employee's salary. Choosing the right employment model and payment method can help you manage costs and keep your international team paid on time.


## Frequently asked questions about EOR vs PEO


### What is the difference between an EOR and a PEO?


The main difference is who legally employs your staff. An EOR becomes the formal legal employer of workers on your behalf, while a PEO shares certain employment responsibilities with your existing company through co-employment.


An EOR is particularly useful for hiring internationally without establishing a local entity. A PEO generally supports businesses that already have a registered presence where their employees work.


### Which do I need to hire abroad?


An EOR is usually the better option if you want to hire employees in another country without establishing your own local company.


If your business already has a legal entity in that country, a PEO or local payroll and HR provider may be suitable.


The best choice depends on your existing business structure, workforce size, budget and long-term hiring plans.


### Does a PEO require a local entity?


Yes, a traditional PEO generally requires your business to have a registered legal entity in the jurisdiction where employees work.


This is because a PEO operates through a co-employment arrangement rather than replacing your company as the employer.


Some providers offer international PEO services without requiring a local entity, but these may actually use an EOR structure. Always confirm the legal employment model before signing an agreement.


### Who is the legal employer under an EOR or PEO?


Under an EOR arrangement, the EOR is the formal legal employer, although your company still directs the employee's daily work and may retain certain legal responsibilities.


Under a traditional PEO arrangement, your company remains an employer, while the PEO assumes specified employment-related responsibilities through co-employment.


The exact allocation of responsibilities depends on local laws and the provider agreement.


### Which is cheaper, an EOR or a PEO?


A PEO may be cheaper per employee for an established business with a larger workforce, but an EOR can be more economical when you're hiring a small number of employees in countries where you don't have a legal entity.


EOR fees often reflect the additional responsibilities and infrastructure involved in international employment.


To compare costs accurately, include service fees, employer taxes, benefits, local entity expenses, payroll charges and any currency conversion costs.


### How do I pay an international team?


You can pay an international team through an EOR, a local payroll arrangement supported by a PEO or direct contractor payments, depending on the worker's legal classification.


For employees hired through an EOR, you'll generally fund the provider, which processes salaries and statutory deductions locally.


For independent contractors, you may be able to use an international payment platform such as Grey to send money to supported countries, subject to account eligibility and payment requirements.
